facts.claim: "Hell Without the Flames" was released as a single on February 13, 2026, and the copyright line says it is under exclusive license to Rounder Records, a Concord Label Group release.
The song is credited to Josiah Leming and Joel Little as writers.
The song was produced by Josiah Leming and Konrad Snyder.

Discogs credits Josiah Leming with acoustic guitar, banjo, classical guitar, harmonica, slide guitar, bass and vocals on the track. Ryan Levine plays drums and tambourine, and Brian Stanley is also credited on bass. Konrad Snyder recorded and mixed the album, and Adam Grover mastered it.
The song was the lead single from the album As Is, released May 8, 2026 on Rounder. It was announced with an official video and with Leming's signing to Rounder.

As Is has ten songs, whittled down from nearly 100 written over about a year. It is Leming's first full-length since 2023's Endurance, and he deliberately went more electric after Endurance rather than make another acoustic record.

Leming said he needed to work quietly away from the internet and pull back for a year to understand what was on his heart. He also said his only goal is to make something real and honest that can get people through the day.
In a Bluegrass Situation interview, Leming said the video for the song was shot in Colombia, because that is where jobs like the ones in the song have moved, and workers there are paid even less.
Americana UK's review of As Is calls the song a portrait of everyday working-class life and says Leming's gravelly delivery conveys the bone-weariness in the lyrics.

Josiah and the Bonnevilles is the stage name of Josiah Leming, a Morristown, Tennessee native now based in Nashville. He left high school at 17 to tour while living in his car, signed to Warner Bros. at 19, and has released music independently since. He completed his first sold-out headlining tour in 2024.

research.lineage: The song sits in the modern folk and Americana singer-songwriter tradition, with a more electric, rootsy sound that critics compare to Bob Dylan.

draft:
"She didn't slam the door." That's the line in **Hell Without the Flames** that tells you what kind of hell this is. Nobody screams. Someone leaves on a Monday, quietly, and the narrator explains why in one more line: "But it was always one day more." A better life was promised for a date that kept sliding, and she got tired of waiting. The song never lets the narrator off that hook. It never lets the narrator fully own it, either.

The title names a damnation without spectacle: a long night shift, a drive home half-dead, cracks in the pavement that turn into cracks in a heart the narrator insists is stone. Josiah Leming, who records as Josiah and the Bonnevilles and wrote the song with Joel Little, keeps the misery ordinary on purpose. When friends ask how it's going, the answer is a shrug about waiting for the world to end. It's the joke people tell so they don't have to say the true thing. Then the chorus says it anyway: "Rat inside a cage holding back the rage." Exhaustion and anger share one body, and the anger has nowhere to go but inward. The last chorus makes it worse. Another hill to climb, another grudge to nurse, and it's night again.

The band doesn't play it as a dirge. A strummed acoustic guitar sets the pulse, the bass walks underneath, and Ryan Levine's drums keep a steady, driving beat. A clean electric guitar traces a melody that answers the vocal line for line. Leming's voice is clear with a little rasp at the edges, and the delivery is closer to talking than pleading. The production, by Leming and Konrad Snyder, is clean and a bit roomy. That brightness is the trick. It moves like a song for the drive home, which is exactly where its narrator is stuck.

It was the lead single from *As Is*, Leming's first full-length since 2023's *Endurance*. This time he deliberately went more electric instead of making another acoustic record, and critics hear Dylan in the plugged-in, rootsy turn. The ten songs were whittled from nearly a hundred, written after he stepped away from the internet for a year. He shot the video in Colombia, he told The Bluegrass Situation, because that's where jobs like the narrator's have gone, for even less pay. That widens the song's sympathy. The cage isn't one person's, and the rage being held back belongs to a lot of people punching the same clock.

Leming has said all he wants is to make something real and honest that can get people through the day. This one does it by refusing to pretend the day is better than it is. It sticks because it hands you a chorus bright enough to sing on the way home, and every time you sing it, you're admitting how tired you are.
